findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes with TypeError on every non-empty datetime page
findings.body: get_item_key copies the numeric logic from Paginator: `value = getattr(item, self.key)` followed by `math.floor(value)` / `math.ceil(value)`. The endpoint sorts by `-datetime`, so self.key is 'datetime' and the value is a datetime.datetime. math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError. build_cursor calls this key on the first result whenever a page has any rows (via _build_next_values), so with `?optimized_pagination=true` from a superuser or global-access user, every non-empty audit log page returns a 500. DateTimePaginator avoids this by converting to a millisecond timestamp. value_from_cursor here also returns the raw cursor integer, which build_queryset would compare against a datetime column even if the key function worked. The optimized path is unusable as written.

findings.title: Negative cursor offsets are passed straight to queryset slicing and raise
findings.body: On the enable_advanced_features branch, `start_offset = cursor.offset` can be negative and is used in `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySet does not support negative indexing and raises ('Negative indexing is not supported'), so any cursor with a negative offset produces a 500. The cursor comes from the client-supplied query string, so an admin can trigger this by crafting a cursor. The comments at lines 876 and 878-879 say Django 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' and that this grants access 'beyond normal pagination bounds'; both claims are false, and the advertised behavior never works.

findings.title: Shared BasePaginator silently clamps negative next-page offsets, leaving cursor arithmetic inconsistent
findings.body: For next-page cursors, the query now starts at max(0, offset), but build_cursor still receives the raw negative cursor.offset. When the key value is unchanged, _build_next_values computes next_offset = offset + limit from the negative value. The returned page therefore starts at row 0 while the next cursor is computed as if it started at a negative position, so consecutive pages can overlap. Before this change such cursors raised an error; now they return wrong pages silently. BasePaginator is shared by DateTimePaginator, Paginator and every other endpoint using them, so this changes behavior well beyond the audit log endpoint. The change is also not a performance optimization, and no tests cover it.

findings.title: Advanced pagination gated on bare User.is_superuser instead of an active superuser session
findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` checks the User model flag directly. Sentry gates superuser behavior on an active superuser session (is_active_superuser(request)), so this bypasses the session-level elevation check. It also introduces a new authorization decision (superuser or global-access member unlocks a different paginator and negative-offset handling) outside the endpoint's permission class, controlled by a client-supplied `optimized_pagination` query parameter.

findings.title: New pagination path and gating logic have no tests and the PR description is empty
findings.body: The PR adds a new paginator class, a new query-parameter switch, a superuser/global-access gate, and changes to the shared BasePaginator offset handling, but adds no tests. The description is just 'Test 1'. A single test requesting `optimized_pagination=true` with a non-empty audit log would have exposed the datetime TypeError in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key. Tests should also cover negative cursor offsets, permission gating for non-admin members, and the unchanged default DateTimePaginator behavior.

findings.title: Performance claims in comments are not backed by any change in query behavior
findings.body: The comments describe the optimized path as 'high-performance' and 'efficient browsing of large audit datasets'. For non-negative offsets the optimized path issues the same queryset, ordering and slice as DateTimePaginator, and it adds no index, query or caching change. The only behavioral difference is the negative-offset path, which crashes. The comments and the PR title overstate what the change does.

findings.title: Comment claims negative offsets are allowed, but this diff changes no code here
findings.body: The only change in Cursor.__init__ is a comment saying it 'allows negative offsets' and 'enables efficient reverse pagination'. The code (`self.offset = int(offset)`) is unchanged and already accepted negative values before this PR. Rejection of negative offsets happens in the paginators, so the comment describes a behavior that does not come from this line and misleads readers about where the behavior lives.
